name: Roro
confidence_why: Strong (1914) puts the accent on the first syllable of two-syllable words and the second syllable of longer ones (or the first when a trisyllable contains a diphthong), Kim and Kim (1998) describe predictable penultimate stress with a four-syllable example stressed on the penult, Kim (2002) writes that stress "basically occurs on the second syllable", and Bluhme (1970) found Roro word stress weak…
catalog_citation: Strong, W. M. 1914. The Roro and Mekeo languages of British New Guinea. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 4(4): 285-311. Berlin: Reimer. (archive.org item afrikaundberse0404meinuoft)
catalog_locator: p. 286, section 'Roro. Accent.' (PDF page 32 of the archive.org scan)
catalog_quote: Roro. Accent. In words with two syllables the accent is on the first syllable. In words with three syllables the accent is on the first syllable if it contains a diphthong but otherwise on the second syllable. In words with more than three syllables the accent is on the second syllable.
readall_conflicts: The one listed work is silent, so nothing new for the listed-works record. But three other Roro/Waima sources already held held by the project disagree with each other on placement, and none of them is in the catalog record (rule empty). (a) Kim, Namsoo & Duckshin Kim 1998, Waima Grammar Essentials, SIL-PNG, §2.1 p.3 (PDF p.8-9 of; SIL archive 43825): "Waima stress is realized by loudness, length and pitch, and it is predictable. Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable in normal words, ie., nouns and adjectives. Noun words consist of the root and any affixes, such as inalienable possessive pronouns, compounds, etc. The example (4) shows the stress on the penultimate syllable of each nominal word." with /kemo/ ['kemo] 'bamboo', /pakoti/ [pa'koti] 'scissors', /bitotiri/ [bito'tiri] 'a bird' — fixed: penultimate syllable, domain = noun/adjective word including possessive suffixes. (b) Waima (Roro) Organised Phonology Data, data checked by Nam Soo Kim 2002, printed 2004, p.2; SIL archive 42313): "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) / Stress basically occurs on the second syllable." — fixed: second syllable, which coincides with penult only in trisyllables and contradicts the 1998 examples ['kemo] (first syllable) and [bito'tiri] (third syllable). (c) Bluhme 1970 (Pacific Linguistics C-13, p.874;, per this folder's of 2026-09-16) reports word stress as rather weak and variable (i'nelana, i'rubuna vs,babe'rona, pero'beta; 'pohama ~ po'hama). Davis 1974 (Kivung 7, p.5-6) gives…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on Strong 1914 p. 286 in the page image we hold and scanned.
